title: SQL / PostgreSQL Data Types
relevance: SDE interviews and OAs probe whether you pick storage types that preserve correctness for money, IDs, text, and time rather than defaulting to floats or naive strings.

phases.goal: Establish the core PostgreSQL type families and when each family is the default choice.

must_hit.point: PostgreSQL provides three integer sizes—SMALLINT (2 bytes), INTEGER (4 bytes), and BIGINT (8 bytes)—chosen by the maximum value you expect to store.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists SMALLINT/INTEGER/BIGINT with byte sizes and says INTEGER is the usual default for general numbers and identifiers.

must_hit.point: DECIMAL and NUMERIC are equivalent fixed-point types defined as NUMERIC(p, s), where p is total significant digits and s is digits after the decimal.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States DECIMAL ≡ NUMERIC, defines precision vs scale, and gives an example like NUMERIC(5, 2).

must_hit.point: Character data is stored as UTF-8; CHAR(n) is fixed and space-padded, while VARCHAR(n) and TEXT are variable-length and not padded.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts CHAR padding with VARCHAR/TEXT and mentions UTF-8.

must_hit.point: Temporal types include DATE, TIME, TIMESTAMP (no timezone), TIMESTAMPTZ (timezone-aware), and INTERVAL (a span of time).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names each temporal type and distinguishes TIMESTAMP from TIMESTAMPTZ and INTERVAL.

must_hit.point: BOOLEAN is a native truth type accepting TRUE, FALSE, and NULL; BYTEA stores raw binary without UTF-8 interpretation.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says Postgres treats true/false as native concepts and uses BYTEA for images/hashes that TEXT would corrupt.

probes: Walk through the main PostgreSQL numeric, string, temporal, boolean, and binary types and when you would reach for each.

hints.1: Start by grouping types: exact integers, fixed-point decimals, floats, strings, time, bool/binary.
hints.2: For each group, name the concrete Postgres types and one typical use (IDs, money, sensors, codes, events).
hints.3: Say INTEGER/BIGINT for IDs, NUMERIC/DECIMAL for money, TEXT/VARCHAR for most text, TIMESTAMPTZ for real-world events, BOOLEAN for flags, BYTEA for raw bytes.

phases.goal: Show how key types actually store and constrain values, including identity, precision, padding, and timezone conversion.

must_hit.point: Auto-incrementing integer keys use GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY so the engine assigns the next unique integer without the application tracking the last value.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY on an INTEGER primary-key style column.

must_hit.point: NUMERIC(5, 2) can store any value from -999.99 to 999.99; REAL (~6 decimal digits, 4 bytes) and DOUBLE PRECISION (~15 decimal digits, 8 bytes) are approximate.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives the NUMERIC(5, 2) range and contrasts REAL/DOUBLE PRECISION byte sizes and digit precision.

must_hit.point: Storing 123456789.12 in a 4-byte REAL may read back as 123456792.00 because the value exceeds ~6 digits of guaranteed precision.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Repeats the REAL failure example with those exact figures.

must_hit.point: CHAR(n) pads shorter values with spaces (e.g. 'CA' in CHAR(10) becomes ten characters); CHAR/VARCHAR max length is 10,485,760 bytes and TEXT is ~1 GB.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains space-padding with the CA/CHAR(10) case and cites the documented max lengths.

must_hit.point: TIMESTAMPTZ converts the input using its offset to UTC for storage and discards the original timezone label; queries translate that stored UTC back to the session’s local timezone.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says it stores UTC, not the original timezone string, and converts on read.

probes: Explain what NUMERIC(p,s), CHAR padding, and TIMESTAMPTZ actually do on insert and on read.

hints.1: Pick one exact decimal definition, one string-padding behavior, and one timezone behavior.
hints.2: For TIMESTAMPTZ, separate input offset → UTC storage from display conversion; for CHAR, talk about invisible trailing spaces.
hints.3: State NUMERIC(5,2) range, CHAR space-padding, and that TIMESTAMPTZ stores UTC and drops the original timezone label.

phases.goal: Force explicit comparison of competing type choices and what each sacrifices.

must_hit.point: Fixed-point DECIMAL/NUMERIC trades speed and storage for exact fractional precision; floating-point trades precision for a wide range in little memory.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses the ledger-vs-spring-scale idea and says floats compound microscopic errors over many transactions.

must_hit.point: CHAR(n) keeps uniform row width but wastes space and forces trimming; VARCHAR/TEXT store only the characters provided (plus a length tag) and are the default unless length is globally fixed.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Rejects CHAR-for-everything because padding wastes disk and breaks naive equality searches.

must_hit.point: Plain TIMESTAMP loses absolute event time; Unix-epoch BIGINT avoids timezone bugs but makes calendar queries (e.g. all Tuesday events) expensive; TIMESTAMPTZ is preferred for real-world events.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names the TIMESTAMP trap, the epoch alternative’s query cost, and TIMESTAMPTZ as the recommended event type.

must_hit.point: JSON preserves exact text (spaces, duplicate keys) but re-parses on every query; JSONB parses once into binary, supports GIN indexing, and is preferred unless exact whitespace must be preserved.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts filing-cabinet JSON with searchable JSONB and mentions GIN.

must_hit.point: Column arrays can outperform a join for simple tag-like lists but violate First Normal Form’s atomic-value rule.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Acknowledges the normalization violation and the performance win for non-joined lists.

probes: Compare DECIMAL vs FLOAT for money, CHAR vs TEXT for emails, TIMESTAMP vs TIMESTAMPTZ vs epoch, and JSON vs JSONB.

hints.1: Frame each as X vs Y: what you gain and what you lose.
hints.2: Tie money to exact cents, strings to padding, time to absolute moments, JSON to parse-once vs preserve-text.
hints.3: Conclude: NUMERIC for currency, TEXT/VARCHAR by default, TIMESTAMPTZ for events, JSONB unless legal exact-text requirements, arrays only for simple non-joined lists.

phases.goal: Apply type selection to concrete schema decisions and known failure modes.

must_hit.point: Never store currency as REAL/DOUBLE PRECISION; use NUMERIC/DECIMAL so summing many transactions cannot drift by cents.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the classic float-for-money trap and names DECIMAL/NUMERIC as the fix.

must_hit.point: Do not use SMALLINT for growing identifiers: the 32,768th user overflows and blocks new registrations; default to INTEGER or BIGINT unless memory is extremely constrained.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Cites the 32,768 overflow failure and the INTEGER/BIGINT default.

must_hit.point: Emails in CHAR(255) can fail equality searches because of invisible padded spaces (e.g. 239 spaces after a short address); prefer VARCHAR/TEXT, and reserve CHAR(2) for fixed codes like country/state.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions CHAR(255) email padding failure and CHAR(2) for ISO-style codes.

must_hit.point: Store unique IDs as UUID or BIGINT, not VARCHAR(36); use BOOLEAN for yes/no flags; use TEXT for article bodies instead of arbitrary VARCHAR caps; use INET for IPs instead of VARCHAR(45).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Recites several cheat-sheet rows: UUID/BIGINT, BOOLEAN, TEXT for bodies, INET for IPs.

must_hit.point: JSONB columns are queried with operators like ->> (extract as text) and @> (contains); arrays use ANY(); enums enforce a whitelist; TSTZRANGE models booking windows with containment checks.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names JSONB operators, ANY() on arrays, ENUM reject of invalid values, and TSTZRANGE @> for meetings.

probes: Given currency, user IDs, emails, events, and a JSON API payload, which PostgreSQL types do you choose and why?

hints.1: Map each field to the cheat-sheet row: money, ID, email, event, JSON.
hints.2: Call out the wrong type for each and the concrete failure (cents drift, overflow, padded spaces, lost timezone, re-parse).
hints.3: Answer: NUMERIC for money, INTEGER/BIGINT or UUID for IDs, TEXT/VARCHAR for email, TIMESTAMPTZ for events, JSONB for payloads unless exact whitespace is legally required.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Use DECIMAL/NUMERIC for currency and exact measurements because floats store approximate binary values and summing many transactions can leave balances off by cents; floats only win when you need a huge range in little memory and can tolerate imprecision.

CHAR pads to fixed width, which wastes space for variable data like names/emails and breaks naive equality unless you trim; VARCHAR/TEXT store only the written characters and should be the default unless the value has a globally fixed length such as a 2-letter country code.

tradeoffs.topic: TIMESTAMPTZ vs TIMESTAMP vs Unix-epoch BIGINT
tradeoffs.strong_answer: TIMESTAMP without timezone permanently loses the absolute moment of a real-world event; epoch integers avoid timezone bugs but make calendar queries expensive; TIMESTAMPTZ stores UTC and converts on read, which is the right default for events.

JSON keeps exact text including spaces and duplicate keys but must be re-parsed on every query; JSONB parses once into binary, drops redundant whitespace/keys, and supports GIN indexing—prefer JSONB unless you must preserve the exact incoming payload text.

tradeoffs.topic: Arrays in a column vs normalized child table
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Arrays violate First Normal Form’s atomic-value rule but can be much faster for simple lists (like tags) you never join elsewhere; use a related table when those values need relational joins or independent constraints.

gotchas.correction: Use DECIMAL or NUMERIC so every cent is stored exactly; float binary representation can make large sums off by a few cents.

gotchas.trap: Using SMALLINT for a growing primary key or user id
gotchas.correction: At the 32,768th insert the column overflows and registrations halt; default identifiers to INTEGER or BIGINT unless you have a proven extreme memory constraint.

gotchas.trap: Storing emails or other variable text in CHAR(n)
gotchas.correction: CHAR pads with invisible spaces, so equality searches for the unpadded string can fail; use TEXT or VARCHAR, and reserve CHAR for truly fixed codes like CHAR(2) state/country codes.

gotchas.trap: Storing real-world events in plain TIMESTAMP (or assuming an application timezone forever)
gotchas.correction: Without timezone context you permanently lose the absolute point in time; use TIMESTAMPTZ, which stores UTC and converts on read.

gotchas.trap: Putting raw JPEG/binary bytes into a TEXT column
gotchas.correction: TEXT validates UTF-8 and can reject or corrupt binary; store raw bytes in BYTEA.
Use the UUID type (or BIGINT for central counters): text UUIDs waste space and slow index lookups.
